replying_to: Replying to NViT: Vision Transformer Compression and Parameter Redistribution
display_title: Official Review of Paper1642 by Reviewer ZWjq

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to prune Vision Transformer models with global and structural pruning with latency-aware regularization. The proposed NVP model achieves similar performance compared with DeiT-Base with much fewer parameters and faster speed, especially on the recent Ampere GPU architectures which support the acceleration of sparse matrix multiplication, i.e, comparing the speed of V100 and RTX3080.
content.main_review:
Pros:

1. The proposed pruning algorithms jointly take latency and structural into consideration, as well as the properties of the hardware.
2. The experimental results confirm the effectiveness of the proposed pruning method. For example, the pruned models are efficient in speed with a little performance drop compared with their original one. The model can also be pruned to different model sizes while outperforming others with similar model sizes.
3. The paper is easy to follow and well-written. For example, Figure 4 is really helpful in comparing the distribution of the parameters of the proposed redistribution method with the previous one.

Cons:

1. All pruned models in this paper are based on a single model, DeiT-B. This cannot validate the generalization ability of the proposed pruning method on other models, but the authors claim the pruning method as a contribution in the paper. I am also wondering why the authors choose DeiT-B as the base model considering that there are already many better vision transformers such as PVT, Swin, and ViTAE. Can the proposed pruning algorithms be applied to these stage-wise models? And can the systematic analysis from the pruning process help to scale the stage-wise transformers considering that these models are largely different from DeiT?
2. In Table 1, the performance of Swin-B is 83.3 accuracy but the official performance in its paper is 83.5. I am wondering how this performance gap comes.
3. The pruned models with various sizes are compared with others in Table 1. However, the superiority of the NVP variants comes from several aspects, which makes the comparison unfair. The first is the larger and better model (DeiT-B) which NVP are pruned from. The second is the distilling loss from DeiT-B. The last but most important is that the training settings of these models are different. According to Appendix A1, the models for pruning are trained with 32 V100 GPUs and a batch size of 144 per GPU (a batch size of 4608 in total) but other models are trained with the batch size of 1024 in total. Besides, if we consider DeiT-B (where NVP variants are pruned from) as a pretraining process, NVP variants need to finetune another 300 epochs on ImageNet-1K, which sums up to 600 epochs totally not to mention the iterations in the pruning process. But the performance of other models like DeiT-B and Swin-B is reported upon only 300 epochs, while more training epochs have been proved helpful for a performance gain in both ViT and DeiT. For example, DeiT-B with 1000 epochs can reach 84.2 Top-1 accuracy while 300 epochs lead to 83.5 accuracy. I am not challenging the classification performance and acceleration of NVP variants, but wish to see a sound comparison, especially under a fair training setting.
4. The authors also propose a new architecture scaling rule in this paper and claim it as a contribution. However, several concerns are raised on it according to Table 3. For example, NViT-T outperforms Deit-T by around 1 accuracy but NViT-T has much more model parameters (6.4M v.s. 5.6M) which generally leads to better modeling ability. Besides, with the model parameters to 86M, the performance gain of NViT-B vanishes to only 0.1 Top-1 accuracy. This trend may demonstrate that the new design rule does not fit large models. Therefore, I am not convinced by the experiments in Table 3 and consider that the contribution of the new architecture scaling rule is somewhat overclaimed.
5. The authors claim that the efficiency demonstrated on ImageNet can be preserved on downstream classification tasks according to Table 4. However, I have some concerns about the experiments in Table 3. First, the model parameters of NViT-T and NVP-T are 6.4M and 6.9M respectively according to Table 1 and Table 3, while DeiT-T only has 5.6M parameters. Second, NVP-T is pruned from a well-trained DeiT-B model, thus inherently seeing more images (more training epochs) than DeiT-B. These two aspects make the experiment less convincing. Third, the authors should consider validating the transferring ability of a larger model NViT-B to support the conclusion.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper makes some interesting points and observations, but as noted in the main review, some of the paper's claims are not well supported. The different settings for training and the marginal improvement in performance raise concerns for me about the soundness of the findings.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1642 by Reviewer ZWjq

content.title: Response to Reviewer ZWjq
content.comment:
We would like to thank you for your thorough review and valuable comments. Hopefully the following responses can address your concerns.

**Q1: Generalization ability on stage-wise models like SWIN-Transformer**

**A1:** We chose to work on DEIT as it was the SOTA method at the beginning of this project, and because few other pruning methods reported results for it. We are excited with the rapid growth of the field of vision transformer, and agree that having a try on pruning multi-stage models like SWIN-Transformer would be interesting. Note that SWIN transformer doesn’t bring additional structural components comparing to ViT, as the novel shift-window attention mechanism is parameter-free. In this case our method can be applied for pruning a single stage in SWIN-Transformer directly without any modification. We show the pruning results and discovered trend of pruning stage 2 of the SWIN-B model in [A2 to Reviewer 6mQe](https://openreview.net/forum?id=LzBBxCg-xpa&noteId=uNU9oInBFiO). 

Applying global pruning on all the stages simultaneously would lead to better accuracy-efficiency tradeoff, yet it involves additional modification to the pruning procedure, which we haven’t got enough time to finish. We will work on this as a future work.

**Q2: SWIN-B accuracy in Table 1**

**A2:** Thanks for noticing this. We took the result from the [Arxiv version 1 of the SWIN transformer paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.14030v1.pdf). Apparently the results have been updated in their final revision, we will make the modification to the table to reflect this change. Nevertheless this doesn’t affect our claims in the paper.

**Q3: Fair comparison between NVP and pretrained models**

**A3:** One motivation of the pruning method, especially structural pruning is to utilize the information learnt by the large model in a more efficient way. Effectively using the knowledge from the full model should be considered as an advantage, not a drawback.

As for the training iteration of the pruned model, the pruning process only involves 20-30 epochs, which is small compared to the finetuning process and accounts for <10% of the full finetuning. To better understand the effectiveness of finetuning, we further finetune the pretrained DEIT-S model 300 epoch with the same objective as NVP (Base model distillation+CNN distillation), which leads to a top-1 accuracy of 82.18. NVP-S reaches similar accuracy while being both smaller and faster.

**Q4: Performance gain of NViT**

**A4:** We believe that accuracy improvement is a subjective matter and even 0.1 is important. As for NViT-T, although NViT-T has a larger model size than DEIT-T, it is still faster on runtime latency (4.53x vs. 4.39x speedup over DEIT-B). Given that the NViT design rule is discovered from latency-aware global structural pruning, we see it as an advantage that NViT can fit in more parameters under the latency budget compared to DEIT. This is achieved by trading the QK V dimension with the MLP dimension, which is discussed in Section 4.1 as one of the trends from the pruned model.

If we further scale down NViT to EMB 176, the model will have the same amount of parameters as DEIT-T. This model achieves 4.75x speedup over DEIT-B, which is 1.08x speedup over DEIT-T. We are training the EMB 176 model now and will provide the result shortly.

**Q5: Significance of the downstream task transfer results**

**A5:** As mentioned in A4, we see it as an advantage for NVP and NViT models to be able to fit in more parameters under the latency budget. As ViT model has been used as a pretrained model on downstream tasks, here we use the NVP experiment to show that this transferability can still be preserved after structural pruning. This result is significant as it shows NVP can be used to generate efficient pretrained models with high performance on downstream tasks.

Due to the constrained time and resources during the rebuttal period it’s hard to finish the base model experiments. We will add it later in our final version.

I appreciate the authors' efforts in solving the concerns. However, some of my concerns remain.

- For the pruning of Swin-B, with 1.67x speedup, the classification accuracy drops from 83.42 to 78.25. However, Swin-T, which is 2.71x speedup compared with Swin-B, obtains over 81 classification accuracy. It seems that the proposed pruning algorithm does not work well on the vision transformers with stage-wise structures. Besides, is it possible to evaluate the performance of the pruned Swin-B on downstream tasks such as detection or segmentation? 

-  The fair comparison concerns still remain. The author claims that using the same training strategy, the pruned NVP-S and the plain DeiT-S obtain similar performance with similar speed and parameters. For the stage-wise model, the pruned models (pruned Swin-B) performance is even worse than the smaller model (Swin-S) and runs slower. Such a phenomenon can not demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. 

-  I am still willing to see the performance of EMB 176 model. Whether the model can obtain a better performance than DeiT-T under the same training settings?

replying_to: Replying to Some concerns should be further addressed

content.title: Reply to your further concerns
content.comment:
We would like to thank you for your positive feedback. Hopefully the following can resolve your concerns.

- For SWIN-B pruning the reported accuracy is achieved without any finetuning, so it’s expected to be lower. We are currently finetuning the pruned checkpoints and will report the results tomorrow.  Also note that we are only pruning a single stage of SWIN for now, so the pruning performance may not be optimal. A more systematic investigation on SWIN transformer pruning and parameter redistribution rule would be a fruitful extension to our work.

- For the DEIT-S finetuning performance, first note that it has benefited from the full model distillation objective, which is one of the key components of this work. Also, for the starting point of the finetuning process, pretrained DEIT-S model has an accuracy of 81.2, while the pruned NVP-S before finetuning has a much lower accuracy of 76.59. Yet after 300 epochs of finetuning with the same setting NVP-S comes on top. This proves our pruned model has a better learnability, which may also contribute to the good performance on downstream task transfer learning.

- For NViT with EMB 176, we train it following the same hyperparameter for 300 epochs, and reach 74.2 top-1 accuracy. This is slightly higher then our reported NViT-T (EMB 192) performance, and is higher than DEIT-T by 1.4% with the same amount of parameters. This results proves that the key for NViT’s high performance is indeed the parameter redistribution, rather than simply more parameters.

replying_to: Replying to Reply to your further concerns

content.title: Reply to your further concerns (continued)
content.comment:
With 230 epochs of finetuning the 60% latency model improved from 78.25 to 82.43, while the 50% latency model improved from 74.82 to 81.67. As we observe more finetuning epochs will lead to a higher accuracy, we will further finetune the pruned models and include the results in the final manuscript.

We would like to emphasize that our work is designed for ViT and DEIT architecture, and extending it to multi-stage models like SWIN may not be naive. Meanwhile, our preliminary exploration of directly applying our method to SWIN transformer already shows interesting observations like more dimensions are kept in earlier blocks and less are in later blocks, and the block with regular window attention (odd blocks) tend to have more attention-related dimensions than neighboring shifted window attention blocks (even blocks). This implies our proposed techniques like full model distillation, latency-aware regularization and most importantly using global pruning to discover parameter redistribution rules can be key building blocks for improving SWIN transformer efficiency in future works. 

We also would like to thank you for the thoughtful and constructive feedback. If you have any further questions, concerns, or comments, please feel free to let us know during the discussion period. Otherwise, we would appreciate it if you considered raising your final rating.

content.main_review:
Strengths:
+ The proposed vision transformer architectures (NVP and NViT) can achieve a better speed-accuracy tradeoff than Deit.
+ The paper presents interesting and informative insights about the model design of vision transformers in Sec. 4.1.

Weaknesses:
- The novelty of the paper is not enough. To me, this paper is only an application of pruning algorithms on vision transformers. I acknowledged that it may need many tunings to make things work well on vision transformers, but these tunings cannot be considered as something novel.
- The paper is only based on Deit, which is too simple and can only be used for image classification. Recently, there are many new vision transformers such as PVT [1] and Swin [2], which are designed for dense prediction tasks (e.g., object detection) and have wider applications. I think the paper should conduct experiments on these transformers, which will be more significant.

[2] Hierarchical Vision Transformer using Shifted Windows.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 6mQe
content.comment:
We would like to thank you for your thorough review and valuable comments. Hopefully the following responses can address your concerns.

**Q1: The novelty of the paper**

**A1:** To the best of our knowledge this work is the first to apply latency-aware global structural pruning on ViT models. The architecture of ViT is significantly different from CNN, so designing the dimensions to be pruned, adjusting the pruning criteria and find appropriate pruning and finetuning objective isn’t trivial. Our work shows the possibility of pruning ViT model by a large portion with a small loss, leading to state-of-the-art efficiency.

More importantly, the parameter distribution rule for an efficient ViT model hasn’t been well studied. We show the pruning result from our global structural pruning can inspire more efficient design of the ViT architecture, where the NViT design rule derived from the pruning observation consistently beating DEIT counterparts while being faster. This has never been attempted for ViT models, and we believe it opens up a new way to better understand the contribution of different components in the ViT architecture, and inspires more efficient ViT models.

**Q2: Pruning performance on SWIN transformer**

**A2:** We chose to work on DEIT as it was the SOTA method at the beginning of this project, and because few other pruning methods reported results for it. We are excited with the rapid growth of the field of vision transformer, and agree that having a try on pruning multi-stage models like SWIN-Transformer would be interesting. Note that SWIN transformer doesn’t bring additional structural components comparing to ViT, as the novel shift-window attention mechanism is parameter-free. In this case our method can be applied for pruning a single stage in SWIN-Transformer directly without any modification. Here we prune stage 2 of the SWIN-B model, which consists of 18/24 of the transformer blocks, 65% of parameters, 75% of FLOPs and 70% of the overall latency of the SWIN-B model.

We provide 2 sets of results with latency targets 50% and 60% of the full model stage 2 latency. The design space, dimensional grouping and pruning procedure are the same as described in Appendix A.2. We utilize the code, training pipeline and hyperparameter setting as in the [official repo](https://github.com/microsoft/Swin-Transformer). Since SWIN does not utilize CNN teacher here we only use full model distillation in the pruning and finetuning process. The results are as follows, we show accuracy before finetuning for now and will update the finetuned accuracy shortly.

| Target | Pruning steps | Stage 2 EMB | Param. (Stage 2) | FLOPs (Stage 2) | Speedup (Stage 2) | Pruned accuracy |
|--------|---------------|-------------|------------------|-----------------|-------------------|-----------------|
| SWIN-B | N/A           | 512         | 1x               | 1x              | 1x                | 83.42           |
| 60%    | 438           | 336         | 1.40x (1.79x)    | 1.48x (1.79x)   | 1.39x (1.67x)     | 78.25           |
| 50%    | 556           | 272         | 1.88x (3.63x)    | 2.12x (3.62x)   | 1.54x (1.99x)     | 74.82           |

As can be seen from the result, our latency-aware global structural pruning can also work well on pruning single stages of the SWIN-Transformer, with the 60% latency model having the potential of achieving lossless compression after finetuning. Yet less can be pruned from the SWIN-Transformer model compared to ViT, showing the model architecture of SWIN is less redundant and more sensitive to pruning.

content.title: Response to Reviewer awr6
content.comment:
We would like to thank you for your thorough review and valuable comments. Hopefully the following responses can address your concerns.

**Q1: Comparing to simple baseline method**

**A1:** In Table 1 of our paper we compared NVP with SViTE, where we show NVP beat it’s compression rate and accuracy, thus naturally beating the simple baselines mentioned in SViTE. Also, we perform ablation study with two simple global pruning baseline: global pruning with magnitude-based pruning criteria and global pruning without latency regularization. The results are provided in [A5 and A6 to Reviewer jSKV](https://openreview.net/forum?id=LzBBxCg-xpa&noteId=ZZ3kvAholt) respectively. 

**Q2: Ablation study with the same module as Chen et al. and  without knowledge distillation**

**A2:** The major difference between NVP and SViTE is that SViTE uses a layer-wise pruning to prune all the structures to the same rate, while NVP enables global structural pruning. Global structural pruning is one of the major contributions of this work as it allows more flexibility in the pruned architecture and the discovery of parameter distribution rules across different structural components. This cannot be done with layer-wise pruning without extensive sensitivity adjustments by hands. Thus we believe that even if we are working on the same module as SViTE, NVP can still reach better efficiency, and can discover similar rules as NViT. 

As for knowledge distillation, as we have mentioned in the ablation study of Appendix B.1, using full model distillation will lead to ~0.2% accuracy gain in the finetuning process. While the results in Table-1 shows NVP-S outperforms SViTE by 0.9%, while having 1.7x less parameters and 1.8x less FLOPs. We think this gap cannot be bridged even if full model distillation is applied for SViTE.

content.title: Response to Reviewer jSKV
content.comment:
We would like to thank you for your thorough review and valuable comments. Hopefully the following responses can address your concerns.

**Q1: Novelty and contribution of the proposed method**

**A1:** To the best of our knowledge this work is the first to apply latency-aware global structural pruning on ViT models. The architecture of ViT is significantly different from CNN, so designing the dimensions to be pruned, adjusting the pruning criteria and find appropriate pruning and finetuning objective isn’t trivial. Our work shows the possibility of pruning ViT model by a large portion with a small loss, leading to state-of-the-art efficiency. 

More importantly, the parameter distribution rule for an efficient ViT model hasn’t been well studied. We show the pruning result from our global structural pruning can inspire more efficient design of the ViT architecture, where the NViT design rule derived from the pruning observation consistently beating DEIT counterparts while being faster. This has never been attempted for ViT models, and we believe it  opens up a new way to better understand the contribution of different components in the ViT architecture, and inspires more efficient ViT models.

**Q2: Ablation study on the NViT design rule**

**A2:** In our paper we do not claim NViT to be the optimal rule that can be designed for parameter redistribution in ViT. Our contribution lies in showing the possibility of finding simple design rules with scalability from global structural pruning results, and discovering the trend for parameter redistribution as in Section 4.1. This is proven by showing that the NViT rule outperforms the naive rule of DEIT when models are trained from scratch under the exact same settings. Hopefully this paper can inspire future works on using our observation for designing more efficient ViT models, such as designing a ViT NAS search space following our parameter redistribution rule.

**Q3: Significance of the explicit head alignment**

**A3:** As our work is focusing on latency-aware pruning, we use runtime speedup as the main evaluation metric of our pruning results. Compared to parameters and FLOPs, latency is more important, as it reflects the throughput and potentially energy consumption of running the model. Explicit head alignment allows fitting more parameters within the latency budget, which is potentially helpful for reaching higher accuracy. While if the head dimensions are not aligned, we may overprune some of the heads, leading to lower accuracy yet no real benefit on the latency.

Besides helping on latency-aware pruning, the reshaped attention block also helps separate the H dimension from QK and V of each head. Later analysis on pruning trends in Section 4.1 shows H, QK and V behaving differently on the scaling with EMB, and having different dimension distribution across different layers. Not separating the H dimension will make the trend observation harder.

**Q4: Performance gain of NViT**

**A4:** We believe that accuracy improvement is a subjective matter and even 0.1 is important. As for NViT-T, although NViT-T has a larger model size than DEIT-T, it is still faster on runtime latency (4.53x vs. 4.39x speedup over DEIT-B). Given that the NViT design rule is discovered from latency-aware global structural pruning, we see it as an advantage that NViT can fit in more parameters under the latency budget compared to DEIT. This is achieved by trading the QK V dimension with the MLP dimension, which is discussed in Section 4.1 as one of the trends from the pruned model.

If we further scale down NViT to EMB 176, the model will have the same amount of parameters as DEIT-T. This model achieves 4.75x speedup over DEIT-B, which is 1.08x speedup over DEIT-T. We are training the EMB 176 model now and will provide the result shortly.

replying_to: Replying to Response to Reviewer jSKV

content.title: Response to Reviewer jSKV (Continued)
content.comment:
**Q5: There is a lack of comparison with other pruning methods**

**A5:** Note that vision transformer is an emerging domain, and this work is among some of the earliest in vision transformer pruning. In Table 1 we already compare NVP with the SOTA efficient ViT method SViTE and AutoFormer. SViTE uses a similar Taylor-importance criteria as ours, but uses manually designed pruning ratio for each layer rather than performing global pruning. AutoFormer utilizes an one-shot NAS method, yet the search space is much smaller than what we explored. Also neither method utilized latency-aware regularization to improve on runtime speedup. So NVP beat both methods on compression rate and accuracy by a large margin, as shown in Table 1.

We also perform an ablation study on pruning with the magnitude-based criteria, where the group with the smallest L2 norm will be pruned in each step. We prune the model to match the latency of DEIT-S, and compare with our NVP-S performance. All the other hyperparameters are set the same. Here we compare the accuracy before finetuning given the limited time available for the rebuttal period.

| Method    | Steps | Param | FLOPs | Acc   |
|-----------|-------|-------|-------|-------|
| Magnitude | 968   | 4.14x | 4.26x | 33.79 |
| NVP-S     | 642   | 4.18x | 4.24x | 76.59 |

It can be seen that magnitude-based pruning struggles to reach the latency target with a larger number of steps, while the pruned model accuracy is much worse. Looking at the remained dimension of the magnitude-based pruning, which is shown in the table below, unveils that most of the structural components are either unpruned or all pruned away (we do not allow 0 dimension in our pruning setting), which infers magnitude-based criteria is incomparable across different structural components and different layers, thus unsuitable for global pruning. As we discussed in Section 3.2.1. This is a well known issue, we are happy to provide additional references if needed.

| EMB | H | QK | V | MLP |
|-----------|-------|-------|-------|-------|
| 768 | 8 | 64 | 8 | 2032 |
| 768 | 2 | 8 | 8 | 2272 |
| 768 | 8 | 64 | 8 | 1568 |
| 768 | 6 | 64 | 8 | 816 |
| 768 | 2 | 8 | 8 | 592 |
| 768 | 12 | 64 | 8 | 464 |
| 768 | 2 | 8 | 8 | 240 |
| 768 | 8 | 64 | 64 | 48 |
| 768 | 2 | 8 | 8 | 32 |
| 768 | 2 | 8 | 8 | 96 |
| 768 | 2 | 8 | 8 | 112 |
| 768 | 2 | 8 | 8 | 48 |

**Q6: Ablation to verify the effectiveness of latency-aware regularization**

**A6:** Here we show the result of pruning without latency regularization, i.e. set eta=0 in Eq. 6 for importance estimation, and compare with our NVP results. Both models are pruned to match DEIT-S latency. Here we compare the accuracy before finetuning given the limited time available for the rebuttal period.

| Eta          | Steps | Param | FLOPs | Acc   |
|--------------|-------|-------|-------|-------|
| 0            | 657   | 4.11x | 4.17x | 74.80 |
| 5e-4 (NVP-S) | 642   | 4.18x | 4.24x | 76.59 |

We can see from the result that pruning with latency-aware regularization can help reaching the target latency quicker, while achieving higher accuracy under the latency budget. To better understand the difference in the achieved architecture, we also show the average dimension across all the blocks after pruning.

| Eta          | EMB | H   | QK   | V    | MLP    |
|--------------|-----|-----|------|------|--------|
| 0            | 416 | 5.7 | 25.3 | 49.3 | 1510.7 |
| 5e-4 (NVP-S) | 400 | 5.8 | 24.0 | 47.3 | 1557.3 |

It can be seen that model pruned with latency regularization tends to have more dimensions on MLP and less on MSA (QK&V), which is in line with our observation made in Sec 4.1 on designing more efficient ViT architecture, where reducing dimensions related to the attention (H, QK, V) while increasing MLP dimension may lead to more accurate model under similar latency.

Thanks for the author's response. Most of my concerns are resolved to a sufficient extent. However, I still have some concerns about the significance of the results and proposed methods.

The NViT models designed following the parameter redistribution rule are basically comparable with the baseline models (but seems to be effective on very small model DEIT-T). This indicates the rule does not work well as expected. Also, can this rule be generalized to different structures?

2. I agree with the fair comparison problem raised by Reviewer ZWjq. The author shows that after finetuning, the baseline model can also achieve a comparable results with the pruned model with similar params and latency. content.title: Reply to your further concerns
content.comment:
Thanks for your positive feedback!

- For your first concern, as our response in A2 we do not claim the NViT architecture presented in Table 2 to be the optimal architecture. NViT is a simple rule inspired by the findings in the trend for parameter redistribution as in Section 4.1, and can already outperform DEIT counterparts. Our contribution here lies in showing the possibility of finding simple design rules with scalability from global structural pruning results. So as NViT rule works on ViT models, we do expect design rules of other architectures, especially transformer-based architectures, can be found via global structural pruning on them. As the first work showing this possibility we hope this can inspire future works on finding efficient design rules on other architectures.

- For comparison with baseline, we would like to first emphasize that our pruning method achieves highly efficient pruned ViT models, beating state of the art efficient ViT methods like SViTE and AutoFormer by a larger margin, as shown in Table 1. Our NVP-B configuration achieves an 1.86x speedup and a 2.57x reduction on FLOPs over DEIT-B with a neglectable 0.07% accuracy drop, which shows the effectiveness of our method on pruning ViT models.  
Finetuning is a common practice in neural network pruning pipeline. We can always finetune a model for more epochs. As mentioned in our further response to [Reviewer ZWjq](https://openreview.net/forum?id=LzBBxCg-xpa&noteId=hv5whpc6xAx), without finetuning NVP-S has a much lower accuracy of 76.59 than the 81.2 of DEIT-S. With 300 epochs of finetuning NVP-S comes on top. Further finetuning of NVP-S will show it beating DEIT-S by an even larger margin.

content.title: Further discussion on PIT and our contributions
content.comment:
Thanks for mentioning the PIT paper. As we carefully read it, we notice that the contribution of PIT aligns with SWIN which identifies the benefits of multistage architecture with pooling in between. 

Our contribution, however, is significantly different. We aim to understand the efficient weight redistribution rule of the ViT model purely in the ViT design space, without changing feature resolution or introducing additional structural components  (CNNs or polling etc). This is achieved with the help of global structural pruning. 

We would like to emphasize our contribution as:
1. The first work to apply global structural pruning on ViT model, swiftly yielding hardware-compatible sparsity
2. Carefully analyze ViT-specific setup and prune all parameters jointly (prior work focuses on one or very few), via detailed ablation of prunable params, carefully designed head alignment and distillation regimes
3. Use it to inspire novel yet simple parameter redistribution rules for NViT. The rule consists of simple and clear changes (see Table 2) that are easy to implement.
 
The success of our method is proved by:
1. Yielding high compression ratio without bells and whistles (~1.9x lossless speedup), as in Table 1 NVP-B.
2. Outperforming by large margin regarding SOTA ViT pruning methods like SViTE by (1.8x further FLOPs compression with +0.9% accuracy gain) and NAS-based method AutoFormer (1.6x further FLOPs compression with +0.5% accuracy gain), as in Table 1 NVP-H and S.
3. Our NViT architecture outperforming DEIT counterparts (up to 1.1% accuracy increase), as in Table 3.
4. Transferring well to downstream tasks (+0.4% accuracy gain on CIFAR-10,+ 0.2% on CIFAR-100 and +2% on iNaturalist), as in Table 4.
5. Generalize well to other architectures, e.g., SWIN (up to 1.7x lossless speedup after full finetuning), as in our [reply to Reviewer 6mQe](https://openreview.net/forum?id=LzBBxCg-xpa&noteId=uNU9oInBFiO) and to Reviewer [ZWjq](https://openreview.net/forum?id=LzBBxCg-xpa&noteId=XhJpobh6ZdB).

These contributions are well recognized by Reviewer [awr6](https://openreview.net/forum?id=LzBBxCg-xpa&noteId=xHUEgtT61OJ) and [6mQe](https://openreview.net/forum?id=LzBBxCg-xpa&noteId=xZPY6O0MgyI).

To the best of our knowledge this work **constitutes a SOTA benchmark for ViT structural pruning**, in addition the first successful attempt that leverages pruning of ViT to redistribute parameters, simple yet works surprisingly well. We hope this can inspire future research on discovering weight redistribution rules on novel models like SWIN and PIT. Our preliminary results in the [reply to Reviewer 6mQe](https://openreview.net/forum?id=LzBBxCg-xpa&noteId=9VHI3gHQroy) already show promising signs on SWIN.

replying_to: Replying to Further discussion on PIT and our contributions

content.title: Thanks for your response
content.comment:
Thanks for the response. I really appreciate the efforts the author made to address the concerns. But I think I am not really convinced by some contributions/claims.

1. Yielding high compression ratio without bells and whistles (~1.9x lossless speedup), as in Table 1 NVP-B.

The author shows that after finetuning, DEIT-S catch up with NVP-S (82.18 vs. 82.19), and the params (22 vs. 21) and latency (2.44 vs. 2.52) are also similar. It seems that the claimed improvement is coming from the finetuning rather than the pruned structure.

2. Our NViT architecture outperforming DEIT counterparts (up to 1.1% accuracy increase), as in Table 3.

The fact is that NViT only improves 1.1% on the tiny setting. On DEIT-B and DEIT-S, the improvement is very marginal (0.11% and 0.22%, respectively). It is very hard to claim that the design rule is effective. Or is it only effective at very small model?

3. Transferring well to downstream tasks (+0.4% accuracy gain on CIFAR-10,+ 0.2% on CIFAR-100 and +2% on iNaturalist), as in Table 4.

As expalined in 1, NVP-T contains finetuning which makes the comparison not fair. NViT-T should be a fair comparison. The improvement is also marginal, CIFAR-10(0.2%), CIFAR-100(0.02%), iNat(1.0%-1.6%). Also, this is only on NViT-T, how about NViT-B and NViT-S? Are they just comparable with DEIT counterparts as in Table 3?

4. About the PiT

I am just giving PiT as an example to show that there are works exploring the design rule for the ViT structure. There are actually many hierarchical ViT that have a different parameter distribution rule from the plain ViT. So I don't think the author could claim that 'this can inspire future works on finding efficient design rules on other architectures.' There are already many works exploring that.

I guess my main concern is in point 1,2,3. Could the author address them here in case I miss something before? Thanks.

content.title: Clarifying your concerns
content.comment:
We really appreciate all the discussions along the way! Thank you for providing the feedback that helped us to realize and better summarize contributions of this work! We would like to summarize the contribution as follows:
1. We achieve lossless 1.9x model acceleration for DEIT-B with the NVP-B configuration, which has never been done before.
2. Outperform AutoFormer (ICCV21) and SViTE (NeurIPS21) [by a large margin](https://openreview.net/forum?id=LzBBxCg-xpa&noteId=b3wILLedgoO). Note that AutoFormer is a more costly NAS method while SViTE uses 600-epoch training in total, so the comparison is fair.
3. Propose important head alignment leading to +0.3% accuracy under same latency budget, that will help future global structural pruning methods on ViT.
4. Used pruning to redistribute parameters. This model is called NViT and achieves 0.1, 0.2 and 1.1% improvement over DEIT models with exactly the same training code and settings. Results do transfer to other datasets.
5. Our pruning technique scales to SWIN out of the box with 1.7x lossless single stage acceleration.
6. With the help of reviewers we create a very important baseline called "fair comparison" that is essentially important to share with the community. Every pruning/NAS technique should at least match it.
 
To further answer your raised concerns (with preserved indexing):
1. - Proposed pruning technique saves training time when multiple models are required. Even though accuracy after finetuning the smaller original model is close to the pruning of the larger model we save at least 1.6x of training time. We provide details on how 1.6x is obtained [in this reply](https://openreview.net/forum?id=LzBBxCg-xpa&noteId=E2pvVtj2hSy).
    - We would like to further verify whether finetuning small DEIT models is helpful universally. We are finetuning DEIT-T for 300 epochs to compare with NVP-T performance. Result to come in a few days.
2. We show that NViT improves DEIT by 0.1% (DEIT-B), 0.22% (DEIT-S), 1.1% (DEIT-T). The value of improvement is a subjective matter, but having improvements for all models is a great sign of consistency. Getting larger improvements for smaller models seems to be reasonable as we are targeting smaller latencies where the architecture matters more.
3. As requested we add additional results on the downstream task transferability of NVP-S, NViT-S and DEIT-S, as follows:
|     Model     |     CIFAR-10 (%)    |     CIFAR-100 (%)    |     INAT 18 (%)    |     INAT 19 (%)    |     Speedup (x)    |
|---------------|---------------------|----------------------|--------------------|--------------------|--------------------|
|     DEIT-S    |     98.52           |     87.07            |     66.79          |     74.22          |     2.29           |
|     NVIT-S    |     98.62           |     87.13            |     66.99          |     74.46          |     2.31           |
|     NVP-S     |     98.78           |     87.90            |     69.10          |     77.00          |     2.37           |

    NViT-S improves DEIT-S by 0.1% on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, and 0.2% on INAT 18 and INAT 19 dataset. NVP-S improves DEIT-S by 0.3% on CIFAR-10, 0.8% on CIFAR-100, and 2.3~2.8% on INAT 18 and INAT 19 dataset. Both NViT and NVP models achieve a larger speedup over DEIT-S. Together with our tiny model results in Table 4 we show that the transferability improvement of NVP and NViT over DEIT is consistent among tasks, and consistent among models.
4. We mentioned in our previous reply that since we aim to identify parameter redistribution rules via global structural pruning, our method can also be used to explore better parameter redistribution rules of hierarchical models as well. For example, how should the dimension of each transformer block be decided within a certain stage of the model? Should the blocks with the shifted window be designed differently than the ones without? These unsolved questions may be answered by future works inspired by our method. Our design rules are derived from the pruning result, and this is what might inspire others: use pruning to discover how parameters should be redistributed.
5. Paper will be improved by providing references to other works that explore parameter redistribution for ViT. We will incorporate the discussion points into the manuscript. We will also be thankful for any provided references.

content.title: Update on DEIT-Tiny finetuning
content.comment:
As suggested we finetuned the pretrained DEIT-Tiny model for an additional 300 epochs. The accuracy improved to 74.97%, which is still lower than the 76.21% achieved by NVP-T, with the same latency. In this fair comparison we achieve 1.24% improvement from the pruning.
  
This result shows that finetuning the smaller model does not lead to consistent performance gain as pruning can achieve. This further proves the significance of our pruning method, in addition to our previous evidence on outperforming SOTA methods and the saving of training cost for achieving multiple efficient models.

Please let use know if this addresses the concern of finetuning original models to compare with the pruned models. We appreciate the feedback on getting these important results.

content.title: Update on smaller NViT model
content.comment: As mentioned in the previous A4 we would like to show more parameter isn't the key of success for NViT-T model with the performance of EMB 176.  For NViT with EMB 176, we train it following the same hyperparameter for 300 epochs, and reach 74.2 top-1 accuracy. This is slightly higher then our reported NViT-T (EMB 192) performance, and is higher than DEIT-T by 1.4% with the same amount of parameters. This results proves that the key for NViT’s high performance is indeed the parameter redistribution, rather than simply more parameters.

content.title: The significance of our work
content.comment:
We would like to thank the reviewers for raising the “fair comparison” questions. We were surprised to find out that finetuning the originally smaller DEIT-S for 300 epochs can reach similar accuracy as the NVP-S. This is true for CNN models as well [1]. However, we would like to emphasize the following two points:
 
1. The rule we found for NViT gives better accuracy under the same training regime, without bells or whistles.
 
2. NVP significantly saves training costs (up to 1.6x for 3 considered models) when multiple models with different latency targets are desired.
 
Expanding on 1: We believe the improvement over Base and Small models are important, whereas the significant improvement over the Tiny model showing our rule is especially useful for scaling down to a more efficient model. This is shown in the 0.1%, 0.2% and 1.1% accuracy gain of NViT-B, S and T over DEIT counterparts in Table 3 of the paper.
 
Expanding on 2: All our NVP models are derived from the same DEIT-B checkpoint, which only needs to be trained once (300 epochs). Then all NVP (pruned) models can be achieved via a single pruning process of ~30 epochs, with each pruned checkpoint snapshot at different estimated latency. A further 300 epochs of finetuning is performed for each pruned model. While training DEIT models from scratch requires 300 initial epochs and 300 additional finetuning epochs (for comparable performance), and also the base model checkpoint for full model distillation. So for achieving NVP-S and NVP-T alone we are saving (300+600 \* 2) / (300+30+300 \* 2) = 1.6x epochs. This saving will only get larger if we are to find more configurations of efficient ViT models via pruning, as NVP is continuous in its target latency space and we can stop anywhere, in addition to the 3 models we compared with. 
 
[1] Rethinking the Value of Network Pruning, Zhuang Liu, Mingjie Sun, Tinghui Zhou, Gao Huang, Trevor Darrell
